source.title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
source.authors: Mark Muchane; Sean M. Richardson; Kiho Park; Victor Veitch

record.tranche_reason: The study compares a hierarchical SAE architecture with a standard SAE and reports improved reconstruction, bearing on whether SAE reconstruction error can shrink with an architectural change. It does not analyze the error's structure or establish that training artifacts are its main cause.
record.gate_note: Figure 3 reports reconstruction metrics for standard and hierarchical SAEs; the paper states that hierarchical capacity improves reconstruction. These results bear on V6's architectural-improvement clause. The CE-loss results do not compare SAE reconstruction against random errors of equal size, so they do not test V3 as worded. The feature-interpretability and hierarchy results do not measure V1–V5.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It proposes a hierarchical SAE (H-SAE) and reports its reconstruction against a TopK baseline on Gemma 2-2B. It does not measure the structure of SAE error: no linear predictability, no per-token error norms across sizes, no comparison with random errors, no error-term ablation in circuits or steering. Its only results are its own method's performance against a baseline, which the rules say are not tests. The comparison is also not matched on total dictionary size, since the H-SAE adds 16 or 64 sublatents per expert. So it cannot show whether dark matter is a training artifact or shrinks under a better architecture at fixed capacity. The Discussion only remarks that reconstruction remains 'far short of perfect' and that it is unclear whether this is a fundamental limit.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say hierarchy 'dramatically' improves reconstruction and moderately improves top-level interpretability, with large efficiency gains. They also note reconstruction is still far short of perfect and that it is unclear whether this is a fundamental limit of dictionary learning.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates a hierarchical SAE with top-level features and expert-specific sublatents, rather than measuring linear predictability or cross-size token-level SAE errors.
record.method_sensitivity: The reconstruction plots vary top-level dictionary size and the number of sublatents per expert (16 or 64).

fits_no_version.finding: At equal top-level latent counts (8k, 16k, 32k) on Gemma 2-2B layer 20, H-SAE lowers 1 - explained variance and the 1 - CE loss score below TopK. The authors say 64 sublatents per expert matches a standard SAE with 4x the compute. Residual error remains substantial, roughly 0.25–0.35 read from the figure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hierarchical, mixture-of-experts SAE architectures reduce reconstruction error at fixed top-level width and compute, without eliminating it.

record.problems: The plotted reconstruction values are not given numerically in the text, and uncertainty estimates are not stated. The experiments use Gemma 2-2B; the study does not measure dark-matter structure directly.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3b's downstream CE-loss comparison is not included because it does not compare SAE reconstructions with random errors of the same size, as V3 requires. Figures 4–7 and the interpretability results in Figure 5 concern feature quality, absorption, redundancy, and hierarchy rather than the versions' stated error properties.

untested.parts: All of it: linear predictability of the SAE error from the input.
All of it: per-token error-norm predictability, shared failure contexts across sizes, and whether error persists with scale.
All of it. CE loss under splicing is reported, but not against random errors of the same norm.
All of it: linear versus nonlinear error components.
All of it: no circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term.
Whether dark matter mostly reflects training choices rather than representation structure. There is no analysis of error structure, no capacity-matched comparison, and no end-to-end training.

record.verdict_notes: The paper does not cite the dark matter paper. The reader's V6 'supports' label is removed: improved reconstruction from a method with more effective capacity does not show that dark matter is a training artifact. Figure 3 panels are swapped in the record: (a) is CE loss and (b) is explained variance. No numeric values are given and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Whether SAE error vectors are linearly predictable from input activations.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, overlap in contexts where different-size SAEs fail, and whether error vanishes with scale.
Whether SAE reconstruction harms model loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether linear and nonlinear error components correspond to unlearned features and qualitatively different, dictionary-resistant structure.
Whether SAE-feature analyses lose model behavior unless the error term is retained.

The study tests reconstruction changes with a hierarchical architecture, but does not determine whether dark matter mostly reflects SAE training choices, whether it is primarily an artifact rather than representation structure, or whether end-to-end training reduces it.

reader_labels.condition: H-SAE versus standard SAE at the plotted dictionary sizes, with 16 or 64 sublatents per expert
reader_labels.reason: The authors report improved reconstruction with hierarchical capacity, consistent with reconstruction error shrinking under an architectural change; the rows do not establish the broader claim that dark matter is mostly a training artifact (R1–R6).
